Chapter 19

Live collaboration: a room, a mailbox and a generator

watchTrip is a query.live — an async generator on the server, a .current in the browser — that yields the whole trip and who is looking at it whenever the room is woken. In-process rooms, a one-slot mailbox so a burst becomes one send, presence with a time-to-live, access asked again on every wake, and the two things that end a stream: the abort signal, and a refusal.

By the end of this chapter

Write a live query as an async generator that ends cleanly, and build the small in-process broadcaster it listens to — knowing what would change to span instances.

Two people planning one trip is the normal case, so the trip is a live query. query.live takes an async generator; on the server it runs for as long as the browser is listening, and every yield is a value the browser sees as .current. During server-side rendering it takes the first value and closes, which is how the trip page has content before any JavaScript runs.

The broadcaster is a Map of rooms, one per trip, and two functions: subscribe and publish. It is in-process on purpose — a single container is the deployment this project ships — and the doc comment names the two ways to make it span instances, Postgres NOTIFY or a Redis stream, neither of which changes the shape. liveRooms exists for the diagnostics page.

Mailbox is the piece that keeps a slow reader from being buried. If ten changes land while the generator is still serialising the last snapshot, it should send the current state once, not ten stale states in a row — so the box holds one pending signal, and put coalesces. next resolves with true for a signal and null once the box is closed, which is how the generator learns that the request went away.

Read the generator as a loop with two exits. Authorise; subscribe, with the room’s listener putting a signal in the mailbox; then forever: load the document, yield it with the presence list, wait on the mailbox — and, woken, authorise again before reading anything. The first exit is the abort signal on the request — the tab closed, the person navigated away — which closes the mailbox, which makes next() return null, which breaks the loop, which runs finally, which unsubscribes. Without that chain every visitor who ever opened the trip would be a listener forever. The second exit is a refusal: readableTrip throws the same 404 it throws at the door, the generator ends with it, and finally unsubscribes just the same.

Why access is asked on every wake, and not once

Because a connection is not a permission. The first version asked once, when the stream opened, and the two people that missed were real: a companion the owner removed while their tab stayed open, and somebody reading the trip by its link after the owner made it private. Both went on receiving every snapshot — every stop, every expense — for as long as the tab lived, and a reload was the only thing that would have shown them the 404. Asking again costs two indexed reads per wake per watcher, on a room of a handful of people; it is the same function, readableTrip, so there is one answer to “may this person read this trip”, given the same way at the door and on every wake. The obvious alternative — have removeMember call watchTrip(slug).reconnect() — cannot work: a reconnect() in a command is a single-flight update for the client that *sent the command*, the owner, and never reaches the removed person’s stream.

It works after a yield, which is not obvious. getRequestEvent() — and so locals.user behind currentUser() — reads the request from an AsyncLocalStorage, and the documentation’s caveat is about runtimes without one: there it “must be called synchronously (i.e. not after an await)”. A generator is worse than an await: its body is cut at every yield, and each piece runs when the *consumer* calls next(), from wherever the consumer is. SvelteKit covers exactly that — its run_remote_generator calls every iterator.next() inside with_request_store, with a comment saying the generator is “chopped apart at each yield” and needs the request context in each piece. A probe in the generator confirmed it before anything was built on it: on every wake, the signed-in person on locals was the right one — Ana, Ben, the companion about to be removed — and after the removal the same call answered with the refusal. What a refusal does in the browser is SvelteKit’s too: the server sends it down the stream as an error and closes it, and the browser’s live query treats an HttpError as final — it keeps the last snapshot, sets .error, and stops instead of reconnecting with backoff. The live chip in chapter 26 then offers “Reconnect”, which asks the server again and is refused again, unless the owner has let the person back in. The end-to-end proof is in chapter 46.

Why the whole document and not a diff

A trip is a few hundred rows at most, the serialisation is a millisecond, and “the client holds exactly what the server holds” is a property worth more than the bytes it costs. There is no client-side cache to invalidate and no merge to get wrong, because there is no client-side copy of the truth — only the last snapshot. Project 4 sent operations and merged them, because a whiteboard has thousands of objects and dozens of editors; a trip does not, and choosing the simpler design where it fits is the skill.

Presence is not data: not stored, not migrated, gone on restart. A Map per trip with a thirty-second time-to-live; a browser touches its entry every fifteen seconds and says goodbye from beforeunload. touch publishes only when something *visible* changed — a new arrival, a pointer on a different stop — because a heartbeat that changes nothing should not wake every watcher. The page-side effects that send these are in chapter 26, along with the loop they must not create.

Checkpoint

  • You can trace the chain from the abort signal to unsubscribe, and say what breaks if one link is missing.
  • You can say why the stream asks for access on every wake, why getRequestEvent() still answers after a yield, and why a reconnect() in removeMember could not have done the job.
  • You can explain what the mailbox coalesces and why a plain queue would be wrong.
  • You know why presence lives in memory and when touch publishes.
